utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Lisa Biersay, on behalf of the Prosecution, and I'm accompanied by Muireann Dennehy, as well as our Case Manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, and our intern as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there's nothing else to be taken care of -- is there anything, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. Yesterday, I addressed the Court about tendering -- seeking to admit 65 ter number 6324 to the exhibit list, and I had indicated that I would consult with Defence counsel. I did consult with Defence counsel, and I fully anticipated trying to convince them of my position, and, in fact, I adopted their position, and we will not be seeking to add it with respect to this witness. It will still stay part of the main motion, but we will not seek to admit it with this -- with this witness, but we will seek another witness through whom to address the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness to be brought in, I'll advise the Court and Defence that I anticipate playing 65 ter number 6200.1, which is a video-clip that is about 1 minute and 15 seconds or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, when referring to exhibit numbers or 65 ter numbers, could you also mention the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour. This one is a video, and it's under your tab number 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Antunovic. I remind --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I remind you that you're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yesterday, you described being confined to your house for six to seven days after the attack on the Dalj police station. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were attending school in Dalj, did you know where the police station was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how far from your school was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I'm having a problem with the sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, could you say your last name for me, please, just so I can test the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Or if the interpreters can say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us? Can the Prosecutor hear us?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, now I can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if we could just go back again. How far was the police station from your school when you were attending school in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in what direction in relation to your school was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Westward, in the direction of the road to Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Zadruga building in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was and it still stands next to the school playground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Next to your school, was there also a church?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Right in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what kind of church was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, I'll ask that 65 ter number 6200.1 be played. And for the Chamber's information, it is an extract of 6200, and it is a video of television footage, and we received this from the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade, and the approximate date we were given was between the 1st and 3rd of August, 1991. And the time codes that we will play will be 00:02:07 to 00:03:24, and we will be playing it and tendering it without the sound. It's merely for the moving images, for the witness to identify.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we pause the video, please. If we could just go back a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you -- we've now stopped the video at 00:03:05. Do you recognise any structure in that frame?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We can continue playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, did you recognise any other buildings other than the -- the church in that video?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was the police station in the condition that you knew it to be in when you were going to school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was destroyed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe what you saw on the video as being the destruction to the -- to the police station.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could see smashed windows, bullet-holes. The interior was demolished as well. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to the video screen, and we're at 00:02:52.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that the building that you're describing as the destroyed Dalj police station?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd move for the extract 65 ter number 6200.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 6200.1 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And while we're here, Your Honour, I would like to move for the admission of the second set of annotations that were made to the hand-drawn map from yesterday. We left with some annotations on the screen at the end of the day, and so I'd move for the admission of the second set of annotations to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P1 marked by the witness yesterday in court for the second time shall be assigned Exhibit Number P4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, yesterday you started to describe how you went looking for your brother after you emerged from your house after being there for six to seven days. Could you describe to the Trial Chamber what you did after you discovered that he was not at his house?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw that my brother wasn't there, or his family, I headed towards Bogaljevci to find my relatives, my aunt and uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By bike.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did you go first?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took an unpaved road in the direction of Pustara where the building of Vodovod was nearby and I was stopped there by soldiers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me where I was headed. I explained to them that I was looking to find my family. An officer appeared. I don't know who he belonged to. And he let me through without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did you go to next?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set out toward Bogaljevci. I was again stopped by a couple of soldiers, asking about where I was headed. I explained to them. Then they asked me whether there was any gunfire in Dalj, whether there was any shooting there. I said that I didn't know, and they let me proceed on my journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached Bogaljevci, and close to my uncle's house, which was empty because they had gone, a civilian wielding a rifle by the name of Sinisa, he was an acquaintance of Bogaljevci, appeared and stopped me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is Sinisa's full name, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glodic, G.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And he was an acquaintance of whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my acquaintance. He was older than me, but I knew him very well. He used to live across from my uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which uncle?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my mother's brother, Josip Suler.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What ethnicity, if you know, was Sinisa Glodic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did he do regarding you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that I should call on his cousin, Stevo Glodic, who was a couple of houses down the street from where he stopped me. I went there. He told me that I was to go to Dalj to be interrogated, that I should get into the van and that nothing -- no harm would come to me, that he would make sure that nothing is done to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said that Sinisa Glodic was wielding a rifle. What do you mean, wielding a rifle? What was he doing with it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he pointed it at me. I got off my bicycle, and I told me -- and I did, just as he had ordered me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did it feel to have someone you knew pointing a rifle at you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a pleasant feeling. I was frightened, of course, as any person would, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You were taken to a van, a nearby van, you said. What kind of van was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just an ordinary van that was used to transport bread from a bakery. It may have even belonged to a bakery, but I don't recall seeing any signs on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to Dalj, near the culture hall, which is by the marketplace in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how far is this culture hall from the school that you used to attend?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 150 metres. Not more, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how far was it from the Orthodox church that you pointed out in the video?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the hall? Two hundred and fifty, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And normally what was that centre used for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large conference hall for wedding parties and similar celebrations, and there was a room upstairs as well which -- I don't know which purpose it served before the event, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, over the weekend, we looked at some photographs of the -- the Dom. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, for some procedural reasons that have nothing to do with you, Mr. Antunovic, we won't be able to use those photographs in the courtroom, but I'd like you to describe to the Trial Chamber as best you can, to paint a picture of this -- of this hall. So if you're facing the building, could you describe to the Trial Chamber what the building looks like.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a building of some 30 metres, perhaps. I'm not sure. There are rooms upstairs as well. In the back is the room for various celebrations, including wedding parties, and further back were the rooms where the prison that I was in later was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if you're facing the building, the Dom, how many storeys is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's the first floor only.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you're standing and facing the building, is there a window anywhere on the building, to the right side?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a window upstairs on one of the sides. That's where the interrogation room was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So could you describe for the Trial Chamber what happened after you were taken out of the van and where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who it was who took me upstairs. At any rate, I was taken to the interrogation room. There was Zeljko Cizmic there. I learned later that he was the policeman in charge there. He interrogated me about the HDZ, about the whereabouts of my brother, about how many Croats there were in Erdut. That was roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How was he dressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know his name at the time. I learnt it later in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you were asked these questions, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the answers, because I didn't really move about the village in the days previously. I didn't know how many Croats had stayed behind. I wasn't able to tell much about the HDZ because I didn't attend any meetings or rallies. As for my brother, I knew that he was not at home, but I didn't know where exactly he had gone to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you gave these answers, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while later, they took me downstairs to the cell, to that prison. As I got in, I observed that there were five or six people there, Croats. I knew them all, but I only recall the family name of one of the men, Fabijancic. He was black and blue, and his lips had been hurt. At any rate, you could tell that he had been injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you know Fabijancic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also used to work for the IPK, the Erdut vineyards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What gender were these -- you said five or six people. Were they men, women?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all men; 35, 40, 50 years old. At any rate, older than me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any other people that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of the day when I was locked up, a father and son by the name of -- last name Susic were brought in. I can't recall their first names. I only know that the orders were given to the son to slap his father about in our presence, for reasons unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who ordered the son to slap his father?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. It was one of those individuals there. There were a lot of them in civilian clothes. Some were in uniform, and one of them gave the order. I can't give you the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "they," are you talking about the prisoners, or are you talking about people who were controlling the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The people who were in power, yes; or guards, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber a little bit about the cell. How big was it, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a small room, 3 by 4, 3 by 5 metres. I think it used to be a pantry of sorts. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there anything on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one or two mattresses and a couple of chairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there a door?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no door, only bars which were locked with a padlock.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point were you taken out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would take us out of the cell, and we would go to work. We had to root out grass from the crevices and such-like tasks. And they then took me to one room to clean and wash the floor. I did that, and a man dressed in civilian clothes was there. I asked him whether they would ever release me, whether they would ever let me leave that prison. He slapped me across my face because his interpretation was that I asked him whether it was possible to run away from there. He took me out of the room into the yard, and he told the other men, soldiers or civilians who were Serbs, that I had asked him whether I could run away. Stevo Glodic arrived there at that moment and told me that he wanted to protect me, but as I was behaving in such a manner, I got what I deserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you returned to the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took me back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the night, some people came. I couldn't call them soldiers because they were civilians as well, but they were Serbs, and they watched over us in prison. They would point a flashlight at a man who had to go out, and he would go for therapy, as they used to call it. One could hear painful cries or whimpers from the adjoining room because that was where they beat people. They would send some people back. Some would remain there longer. Some would leave and then come back. Some did not come back at all. But once they came to the door, they would point a flashlight into someone and that particular person had to go out and he was to be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you taken out and beaten that night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that night. They didn't beat me that night at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morning started with insults through the bars. Whoever it was, a child or an old man, they would shout at us, spit at us, swear our Ustasha mothers, and then we had to go to work again. We did get some breakfast, I have to say, but we had to -- we had to go and perform some work, whatever it was. Some small tasks. But we had to be close to them, and they were able to provoke us and beat us. Two young men noticed me at that time. Later, I learned that they were from Prigrevica, which is a populated place in Serbia. One of them was a blonde with light blonde hair. They called him Ferenc. He was a Hungarian. Or maybe they called him Madzar, which means a Hungarian. That was his nickname. And Ferenc was his name probably. There was another one with black glasses and a big scar on his face. I'm not sure on which side of his face. The two of them took me to a room and ordered me to take off my trousers and my shoes or sneakers, whatever I had on my feet. Then I put my feet on a chair, and with a bat, they beat me on my foot soles. The pain was awful. And you cannot defend yourself, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you remember for how long they beat you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say how long it took. Maybe I would exaggerate if I said five minutes, but in any case, 10 or 20 blows. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So could you explain a little bit. How did you position your feet on the chair?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put up my feet and put them on a chair, as if I put them on the desk now. So as my feet were up on the chair like this, they would hit me with a truncheon on both sides of my feet as hard as they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When they stopped beating you, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they stopped beating me, they ordered me to go to a cellar which was filled with water. The water was cold, and it was between a metre and a half a metre deep, and they ordered me to wash myself. I had to bathe and dive, and they were laughing at me. That was fun for me. Then they gave two buckets to take some water from the basement and to go and clean the toilets, actually the two toilets which were out in the yard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: This was fun for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you had to wash yourself, did you have your clothes back on or were you still undressed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I had put my trousers on. So I had to wash myself fully dressed. Whatever I was wearing, a T-shirt and the trousers and sneakers on my feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you clean the toilets?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the toilet, and I carried water because there was no water there. I had to clean faeces with my hands, and after that when I finished with dirty hands, they gave me bread to eat as if I were supposed to spread that on the bread and eat it, which I did in a way because I had no other option.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you -- how did you feel physically when you had -- after the beating and you had to carry the pail and clean the toilets?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pain in my soles was awful, so I had to put my feet on the side, so to speak, and try to walk in that way, but I just had to do all of that because I didn't know what would come next.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point were you taken back to the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the cell. And after a while, I'm not sure whether it was an hour or two, they took me out again and took me upstairs to Zeljko Cizmic to be questioned again. When I got there, he asked me why I was wet. I told him what had happened, that I was forced to throw myself into the water in the basement, and he then swore at them, swearing their Chetnik mothers, but I think he was doing it just for the sake of form, because he must have known what was going on. Stevo Glodic was also present upstairs at the time, and Zeljko Cizmic told me that I would be released and that Stevo should give me a lift in his car. I refused that -- or, rather, I said that it wasn't necessary and that I could go on my own, because I was afraid where Glodic could take me, kill me someplace, but he could have done it anyway. But these were my thoughts. So they agreed. They said I could go on foot, and they gave me a pass in case I was stopped by the military or anybody else at the check-point so that I could go home. This is how I left. I was stopped in two places by civilians. I showed them the pass I had, and I had no problems. I reached Bogaljevci where I left my bike. They gave it to me, I took it, and I went back home to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At any point during your detention did they, the people who were interrogating you, did they ever tell you that you were being charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood, the biggest problem was that I was a member of the Croatian Democratic Union, their youth organisation, and probably also the fact that I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you left, did you go home?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went home. And a few days later, I'm not sure how many days, but when my feet were better, I went to work at the IPK Osijek vineyards, and I worked there up until October, and then they came for me in a red Yugo car. It was the Krajina police. They came during the night. As far as I remember, they were Zoran Oljaca, Tihomir Ivosevic, and Goran Djakovic. They came in front of the house and when I saw the lights, I was more or less aware of what that was. I was frightened and they told my aunt who opened the door that I needed to go to the station in Erdut to be questioned and that they would bring me back soon and that she shouldn't worry at all. However, once I got into the car, Goran Djakovic sat together with me on the back seat, and he hit me several times with his hand on my temple, and he swore at me. The way to the station is short, and once we arrived, they took me out of the car. Oljaca kicked me in my bottom, close to my spine, and sent me inside into a room where I had to -- to wipe my feet against a Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, you said that you saw the -- let me just find the ... That they took you to the station. What do you mean by "the station"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they called it a police station in Erdut, but there was no inscription on it. There was nothing distinguishing. It was a house with several rooms. When Mr. Bosko Bolic was there, I guess he was the commander at the Erdut police station. I was asked questions again. Everything was the same, the HDZ, the Croats, the weapons, who had what, was there anyone who was opposing or who was prominent as a Croat. Nothing different. Milorad Stricevic arrived there as well. That was the first time I saw him and I didn't know his name at the time. I learned that later. They drove me to Dalj once again, to the same prison where I had been held the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did -- how long did you actually spend inside this house that they were using as a police station?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A short time. Perhaps ten minutes or so. Not long.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And either before or while you were being placed in the car to leave, did anyone say anything to you about Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the car, as far as I remember, Stricevic told me that I should have a last look at Erdut, because I would probably not see it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that I wouldn't be coming back, that they would probably kill me. I don't know what else I could have thought. I was really frightened, of course, but I couldn't find any help anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you said you were taken to the same place in Dalj, what place is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same place, the culture hall. They first took me to a room to be questioned. It was the same room where I had been the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who -- did someone question you this time as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This time it was Stricevic. I did not see Zeljko Cizmic. Stricevic was the man in charge, and it seemed to me that he was the Commander-in-Chief. I company not remember exactly. I think that he slapped me a couple of times, but I'm not sure if that was at that particular moment when they took me in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the room where you were being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Ferenc, the Hungarian from Prigrevica was present. And I think that Arkan was also there on this occasion, because I know that he asked me whether I knew who he was. I told him I didn't. Then he slapped me and introduced himself to me as Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, the leader of the Delije football fans' group and also the leader of the Serbian Volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I apologise. I apologise. That was on the following day. My apologies. Is that not a problem? I made a mistake. I apologise. Stricevic and Ferenc were present, and after questioning, they took me back to the same cell where I had been before, and Arkan was not present there at that time. So I apologise. I did not say that right. I was taken to a cell, and there were two men inside. I could not discern who they were because it was dark, but after a while I could see that they were from my village, Goran and Kosta Surla. They were Serbs. And we talked. I asked them why they were here, and Goran told me that the problem was that they said that his father Kosta took food and drink where the ZNG was in Erdut, that he brought food and drinks for them, which he had to do. This is what I learned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to give us the names again. You said Goran and Kosta Surla?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surla. The last name is Surla.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How do you spell Surla?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S-u-r-l-a.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Goran Surla, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father was called Kosta, and so eventually his nickname was also Kosta, but his father's first name was Kosta, and after him he was nicknamed Kosta as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you present for any exchanges between the two Surlas and the guards, present for conversations between them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Goran Surla was angry. He swore and threatened the guards, telling them that when Arkan arrived the next day that they would be punished for having imprisoned him and that he knew that they would be released which happened indeed the next morning. Arkan arrived. He shouted at the guards, at everyone who was present at the moment. They released Kosta and Goran Surla. I asked this gentleman Kosta to call my aunt and tell her that I was alive because she didn't know where I was and to ask her to send me some cigarettes if at all possible, and he really did do all that, and perhaps some two days later I got some cigarettes. They were brought to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which Kosta did you have that conversation with, the son or the father?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the father.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you eventually that day brought to the interrogation room again?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On that day everything was normal. I worked. I was in the cell. In the evening I was taken upstairs for questioning. And upstairs were Stricevic and Arkan came on that occasion. There was another strong man. I learned later that he was Arkan's soldier. Ferenc was present as well, the Hungarian I mentioned, and some other people. My neighbour Marinko Lucan was also being questioned by them upstairs. He was standing. They brought me in, and they asked me the same questions all once again. Then Arkan told me to come next to him. He asked me if I knew who he was. I said I didn't. He then slapped me and introduced himself to me. He told me that he was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, that he was the leader of the Delije and the Volunteer Guard. Then they ordered me to lie down, they gave me a pencil and a piece of paper, and they told me to make a list of the Croats who remained in Erdut or even better who was armed. I told him that I didn't know who had weapons, and then my neighbour Marinko Lucan said that he knew that Vinko from Erdut was armed. Some people went out of the room. He told them the address. They left to get Vinko. I was lying on the floor all along. They gave me a pencil and a piece of paper, and I made a list of people who had stayed in Erdut, though I didn't know many, and the people I knew were mostly elderly. After a while when I had written something, Arkan told me to get up. I did. I gave him the piece of paper. He said that he couldn't read it and that I had to write it in Cyrillic. So I laid down again and the strong man who was there, I learned later that he was one of Arkan's soldiers, he tread on my back, and it was impossible to write. And the worst of all was that I'm not really well-versed in Cyrillic. I don't know how to write in Cyrillic. I made some attempts. Arkan told me that once again he could not read it but that there was enough time and I could learn both to read and write in Cyrillic really well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said a strong man, that he was standing on your -- treading on your back. How would you describe him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very big man. I would say he must have weighed 100 kilogrammes. He was treading all over my back, and as I said, I was making attempts to write, but that was impossible. I don't remember any longer how he looked. I cannot remember his face. I did not dare to look up. I was frightened, and the whole situation was such that I couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At the time, how much did you weigh when he was stepping on your back?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I weigh 61 or 62 kilos at the moment. I didn't grow much fatter since then. Perhaps I had 5 or 6 kilos less, but it was thereabouts, more or less. I was always small and weak. I guess I was -- I weighed 57 or 58 kilos. I wouldn't say it was any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how tall were you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm 160 centimetres tall now. I doubt that I grew much since then. Perhaps I may have been 3 centimetres shorter, so let's say 157 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that Marinko Lucan gave the name of Vinko Kovacevic. Did you see Vinko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After a while they went to Erdut to get him. Perhaps half an hour or 45 minutes later they arrived with him. He had already been beaten, probably in the car or whatever he was transported in, but one could see that he had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the -- the cell for the second time, how long did you stay total there in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourteen to 15 days and nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And during that time were you -- were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every day, as I told you the first time, whoever passed by, he would call you to come to the bars on the door, and they would slap you, hit you, spit on you, whatever they wanted to do. No one prohibited them from doing that. They had all the right. They wanted to assume. Soldiers and civilians entered sometimes. Outside we had to work in the yard. They beat us quite a lot. On one occasion they took me to a room, one of the bigger rooms in the yard. Two men were there. I cannot remember any longer if they wore civilian clothes or uniforms. And they beat me with a truncheon and with some sort of cable. It was very hard. I'm not sure if it was a telephone cable, but it's very hard, harder than the truncheon and they would hit me by turns, one and then the other. As soon as one hit me, the other would slap me again. I sometimes put my arms up to protect myself, but then they would hit me even harder. The pain was awful. I then had to kneel down and write some stupid things. There was probably no reason for them to keep me there, just so that I would write down who was present in Erdut, who had any weapons. And that was repeated on so many occasions, even though there was nothing for me to write, but I had to make a list of the elderly who had stayed there, because as I said, there were few young people left. Then, once, one of them cut my hair with a bayonet or --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Antunovic. We'll take it one step at a time. How long was your hair when you were arrested in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my hair reached beyond, let's say, the middle of my back, further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber how it came to be that you had your hair cut while you were being detained in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, one of the men cut my hair with a bayonet or a blunt knife. I was kneeling down writing this list. He took hold of my hair, and then he was sawing it off rather than clipping it, really, but of course it hurt me far less than the blows I had received earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time where you had to sing songs while you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. That's quite leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there -- did you have a tattoo when you went -- when you were detained in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a tattoo of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, on my right arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point something happened to that tattoo; is that right? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber the sequence of events that lead up to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was outside in the yard working when one of the people, the Serbs, ordered that I should get up into the cab of the military truck that was parked in the yard and that I should get up there and sing the Croatian song "Rise the Ban," as far as my voice would carry, and I did that as -- as a rifle was pointed at me. And then I was supposed to sing the Yugoslav anthem, which of course I knew, and I sang it. Then they ordered me down from the truck. There was the Ferenc, the Hungarian, and Sinisa Glodic. Sinisa Glodic told me then that I should take my T-shirt off and show them the HDZ tattoo. I did as I was told and then he kicked me and punched me and threw me around like a sack. He asked me to show him the tattoo that I had of the Croatian coat of arms, which I didn't have, in fact. He continued beating me, although I couldn't show him the tattoo I didn't have. Then the Hungarian Ferenc told me that I had one or two days before he returned to get rid of the HDZ tattoo. As soon as I stepped into the cell, the prison, I took my cigarettes and started burning off the tattoo. It took several cigarettes, two or three, that I burned on me that day, and what was formed was a very dark scab that I hoped had gotten rid of the tattoo. The next morning as I woke up, I stripped the scab or the skin off. It hurt terribly, but I had to get rid of it. You could still see the tattoo, and then I kept on burning the tattoo off until it was gone. Several days later, the Hungarian Ferenc showed up. I showed him my arm to -- for him to see that I had gotten rid of the tattoo, that he didn't have to cut off my arm. So although it caused me a lot of pain, still, I got to keep my arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened to the area that you burnt, today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see the scars, the scar where I was burning the skin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you, while you were being detained, did you hear of anyone being referred to as a Vojvoda? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you have any interactions with the person who was called Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a rainy day a man appeared, a soldier, wearing a rain coat. He stopped by our cell. He called out me, Vinko Kovacevic, and Lucan - Marinko Lucan - who was kept with us. He ordered us to slap one another and to give each other as many slaps as one had years. They -- he ordered, however, that we should not use the palms of our hands. And of course there was this lingering anger at Marinko Lucan for telling off on that person earlier on, so I slapped him, but Vojvoda or the Duke would then, as a punishment, give me another slap. So we actually got double the amount of slaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how would you describe the -- this Vojvoda? What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a tall strong man. As I said, he was wearing a rain coat. He was clean-shaven, groomed, not at all neglected in any way. He was every inch a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that: "There was this lingering anger at Marinko Lucan for telling off on that person earlier, so I slapped him." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was that anger, perhaps, and I may have gotten carried off by the fact that he slapped me in turn. I suppose that's how a man gets carried away by these things. It must be the instinct, I don't know. He was taken to prison before I was, and I heard later that he talked about me and about the HDZ. So it in fact turned out that he had been talking about me as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you have any other interactions with this Vojvoda after he slapped you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of it all, after we did as we were told, he called me to the bar door and offered me a cigarette. I took it, lit it. His demeanour was even friendly, if you can call it that way, and he said that for as long as he was there, nobody would be allowed to lay their finger on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened later on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a while, three or four of Arkan's men arrived. The prisoner guard opened the cell for them. They stepped in and kicked us with their boots. I was dealt a blow to the left side of my face, whereas Vinko Kovacevic received several blows including a blow with the heel right below his eye and his skin there cracked. He fainted at that point. As he came to, he was disoriented. He didn't know where he was. We asked the prison guard to fetch some water. He was given some water, washed his face, and pulled himself together. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know anyone by the name of Matija Hum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People would come to the prison in that period of time. There was a person from Aljmas -- in fact, he was from Osijek but had weekend cottage at Aljmas. He was brought in one day. He was around 70 -- 60 or 70 years old. They beat him up as well. One evening they took him out of the cell, the Arkan's Men, I mean. They banged his head against the wall repeatedly. They punched him and kicked him. He never returned to the cell again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity Matija Hum was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described to the Trial Chamber that you were made to and the others were made to work around the premises of the prison cell where you were held. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe to the Trial Chamber what types of work did you do.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Several days later, Marinko Kovacevic and I were left alone in that cell. We were told that we would not be beaten any longer, that we would be a labour group, if you will, so that if a truck came in carrying cargo of potatoes or peppers or whatever, we would unload the food and take it to the nearby store. We would also chop wood. We first went to chop wood at Milorad Stricevic's. We were even given a cup of coffee there. On another occasion, we went to another man's house. His last name was Trbojevic. I don't recall his first name. We chopped his wood and then stacked it up. And there was lady there, his wife - I don't know - who gave us lunch. Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In one minute, Mr. Antunovic. You said Mr. Trbojevic. What ethnicity was Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the house where you worked for Mr. Stricevic, where was that in relation to the prison cell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very close. I don't know if I could gauge it in metres, but it was quite close to the prison. Let's say 500 metres, but I'm not sure at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the occasion where Arkan came in and the Surlas were released; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were chopping wood at Trbojevic's, on that occasion -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber about your interactions with Arkan previously. Did you see Arkan on other occasions, other than the ones that you've mentioned already? So if I were to ask it perhaps a more succinct way, in the -- in the two weeks that you were there, how frequently would you see Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw him when he spoke to Milorad Stricevic, when they were talking about releasing me from gaol. Stricevic was in favour of my release, whereas Arkan said that I should not be released because as I grow older, I would become a Ustasha. And he said if I should ever catch him, I would certainly not show him that sort of mercy. At any rate, it seems that Stricevic prevailed and I was released that evening. There was another person there - I don't know his name - a man who brought a piece of paper to me, a pass which meant that I was going to be released, and I was happy as a child, and in fact I was released that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were still detained in October 1991, you said that there were many different types of people and they were dressed differently. There were some people who were dressed -- who were civilians and others who were dressed in uniforms. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. There were people in civilian clothes. There were people in camouflage, multicolour uniforms. When I was in prison, I didn't observe any regular soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how were the Arkan's Men dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I would see them, they wore the multicolour camouflage uniform and dark black caps, I believe. They were all clean-shaven and well-groomed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Over the two weeks that you were detained, did you have occasion to see Arkan interacting with other people who were controlling the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him that once with Stricevic, as I said, and I think that they were in contact, and I mean Arkan and Stricevic. I say this because whenever Arkan was not there in Dalj, in prison, Stricevic was in charge. Everyone obeyed him. He liked to be addressed as "Colonel, sir." I've just remembered that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And by that, to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stricevic. Stricevic was the one who liked to be addressed as "Colonel, Colonel, sir."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how, based on your observation, did people behave with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my experience, with fear. Everyone obeyed him. I had never heard of anyone standing up to him, save for that conversation which had to do with my release, but that was probably the result of an agreement between Arkan and Stricevic rather than opposition. I had never heard of anyone going against what he had said, at least from what I was able to experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were describing how you were taken from your -- your home - this is for the October 1991 detention - you described then as Krajina police. Why do you call them Krajina police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area was called SAO Krajina at the time, and everybody called them the Krajina police. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: During the time of your detention in October 1991, were you ever told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that the two reasons were the HDZ and the fact that I was Croat. I don't think they needed any other reasons at the time. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know someone named Hinko Gobina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hinko Gubina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how would you spell the last name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: G-u-b-i-n-a.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know someone by that name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the 14/15 days I was there, a man was brought in that I had never seen before. He was beaten up quite badly and did not spend a long time with us in the cell. He spent one or two days there. He was taken away. I never saw him again, nor did I ever hear of him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where is it that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cell. He was there together with me and Vinko Kovacevic. As I said, he was brought in, but was there for one or two days only. I don't know where they took him from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask my friend for a reference in any of the disclosure concerning this person's name?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Certainly. I will get that for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know the name of a person called Pavel Bek?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard the name, but I never saw the man. He was someone they were looking for, searching for in the prison. I recall them calling out his name, but I had never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I seek some guidance from the Trial Chamber whether this is a good time to stop or shall I start a new segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If it's a good time for you, we can stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It would be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness be brought out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will take the break and we will be back at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, two things: You have used so far 2 hours 15, and I think you were asked for a reference by Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. And he was given that reference. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, I'd ask for 65 ter 2860, which is tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Antunovic, I'd just ask you to look at your screen for the image that appears. And this is a photograph. Do you recognise the person depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Stricevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the way he appears in this photograph, is that consistent with the way you saw him in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The face does, but when I saw him, he was mostly wearing a black leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter 2860.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2860 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now requesting 65 ter 2830, tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is a photograph. Do you recognise anyone depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Milorad Stricevic, the one with the glasses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where is Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan is the taller one to the left who is pointing with his finger and who is bare headed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the two men that you've identified, Arkan and Stricevic, is this photograph consistent with how you saw them in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'd move for the admission of 65 ter 2830.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit P6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd ask to be played 65 ter 4802.1, which is tab 17, and this is an extract from 65 ter 4802, which is a video from November 1991. And this was -- this document was received -- this item was received from the Defence in the Dokmanovic case. It was seized from Toma Fila in that case. And the clip that we're proposing to play, 4802.1, the time codes to be played will be 00:10:30, and we'll go to 00:10:57. So it's very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, did you recognise anyone in that clip you just saw?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised Mr. Hadzic, Arkan. And I would ask you if I could watch it once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So we'll now play again 4802.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Milorad Stricevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the record, the clip is also stamped with the date 20/11/1991. At this time, could we see 4802.2, which is tab 18. And then we'll also ask for .3 and .4. They're all related to the video. And that's tab 18, 19, and 20. [Microphone not activated] In that case, we can start with .3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're trying to locate in e-court .2, but we do have .3 ready. So I propose that we play .3 and then .4, so tab 19 and 20, and then we can go back to .2. And for the record, this photograph bears 20.11.1991, with a time code of 14:26.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, do you recognise the document before you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Milorad Stricevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now if we could see 4802.4, also an extract from the clip previously shown. And for the record, in the lower right-hand corner it's 20.11.91, and the time code 14:29.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, do you recognise anyone in this photo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. He is the man facing the camera. He's turned with his face right towards the camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time I'd ask if we have 4802.2 available. If not, we can do it the old fashioned way using the ELMO. Ah, perhaps we could try 048, or without the 0, so just 4802.2, and if not, we can also use the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this the one, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ah, indeed. Thank you, Your Honour. And for the record, this bears the numbers 20.11.91, a time code of 14:25, also an extract from the clip previously shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Zeljko Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you say Zeljko Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My apologies. Goran Hadzic. I apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So at this time we tender 4802.1, 4802.2, 4802.3, and 4802.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a point for the record: The 4802.3 does not reflected what the witness has testified was the name of the person. It should nevertheless be corrected. The first name is wrong. It just says "Ermin" instead of "Milorad." And while I'm on my feet, Your Honours, a correction also for the record. The photographs or the video in question was not seized from Mr. Fila. It was handed over by Mr. Fila. I'm sure it was just a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's a term of art we use internally and it's often the subject of much discussion, but your point is well taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 4802.1 shall be assigned Exhibit P7. 65 ter 4802.2 shall be assigned Exhibit P8. 65 ter 4802.3 shall be assigned Exhibit P9. And 65 ter 4802.4 shall be assigned Exhibit P10. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, when was your birthday in December of -- excuse me. When was your birthday in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My birthday in 1991. Well, frankly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of December, 1973.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on the 23rd of December, 1991, how old did you become?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Seventeen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you become 17 or did you become 18? Let me ask you a different question. In December of 1991, around Christmas time did something happen to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of December, while I was working at the IPK vineyards, they came to get me again with the same -- I guess it was the same red Yugo, and they requested that I go with them. It was the police, policemen from Erdut. Zoran Oljaca was in the car. I don't know who was driving. I cannot remember. I'm not sure. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The 25th of December, was that a religious holiday?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what holiday was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Catholic Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When is the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 7th of January, the 6th or the 7th of January, the first month.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where were you taken this time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to the police in Erdut, which I mentioned earlier, the building, that is. And they came there for me in a jeep, two Arkan's Men, and they took me to the place where Arkan was stationed with his unit, his troops. It was a training centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to a room upstairs for questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there anybody else in the room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An elderly woman was in the corridor in front of the room - she was Manda Maj from Erdut - and an elderly man whose last name was Simak. I don't know and I don't remember his first name. They brought me there at the time and they handcuffed one of my hands with the hand of Maja Manda [as interpreted]. Two girls came along, young girls, and they hit this elderly woman, Maja Manda, on her face with a truncheon. I don't know why. I heard later that her guilt was that she celebrated the Catholic Christmas and that she decorated the Christmas tree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you attached to her when she was being hit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was handcuffed to her, and it hurt me because the handcuffs were stretched, but it was worse for her, I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point were you separated from her?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They separated me from her, and I entered the interrogation room. Milorad Stricevic was inside. He asked me whether anything was going on in the vineyards or in the village, whether anyone was saying against the authorities or the Serbian police, whether anyone made himself prominent by expressing his Croatian feelings. I had nothing to answer him. I told him that I worked with both Serbs and Croats and that no one discussed politics. He then said that I should be taken out and that they would call me later, and that I should try to refresh my memory and think whether I had anything to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you have something to tell them later?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, they took me in, and I remembered, because I was thinking very fast, and I remember the man who had been working in the vineyards and had been taken away a fortnight ago. In any case, I hadn't seen him in the meantime. He was shaven in such a way that his beard was in the shape of the letter U as in "Ustasha," and when I said that, one of the soldiers hit him with Arkan's truncheon on the neck, and he told them not to beat me. He would not allow that. He said that this man was a resolved case, that they had finished with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "he," "He told them not to beat me. He would not allow that --"

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Stricevic told the soldier not to beat me, and Milorad also said that the man I was talking about was a resolved case and that they had finished with him. But I guess it was clear to him that I was honest, and he offered me a cigarette and a glass of water, and he told them to let me go home. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you see anybody else that you knew that day at this location?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They then brought Jura -- Jure Zoretic. He thought that I had reported him for something. I did know him from work, but I did not know anything about him privately, so to speak. So he swore at me, but I was released, and I had absolutely nothing to do with his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When was the next Catholic holiday?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next time was around Easter in April. I don't remember the date, because this is a movable feast.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And April of what year?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe the event that happened to you and your aunt and uncle around Easter, April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I was still employed. I went to work at the IPK vineyards. My aunt worked privately with a lady, and my uncle worked on his tractor in another location. We did not work together. And there were rumours at work that day that Croats from Erdut, Dalj, and other places would be forced to leave for Osijek. We received our salaries that day. I think dinars were still in use as the currency, and we got home at about 3.30 p.m., and I told my aunt that I had heard that there would be expulsions. Not much time passed, and a jeep stopped in front of her house. A man wearing Arkan's uniform got in, told us to pack the essentials, and that we would be leaving for Osijek and going to Tudjman, as he said. I went to one of the rooms. I took a suitcase. I packed trousers and two different socks because I was frightened. I wanted to leave the house as soon as possible. Not far from our house a bus was waiting, and the Croats from the village were inside. I also got on the bus. It was driven by a Serb from Erdut whose name I don't remember. More soldiers entered the house as I was leaving, and they were inspecting the rooms. In one of the rooms, which was a sleeping room of my aunt and uncle, there was a photo of my uncle's son in the uniform of the Yugoslav navy, and this -- Arkan's Men asked who that was. My uncle explained that that was his son, and he said, Well, congratulations, something to that effect. And then saw on a cupboard some knives. It was a package with several knives which are used for killing pigs. He asked my aunt and uncle what that was, and they said that these were the knives for killing pigs. I don't know what he said, but that was the end of it. And my aunt and uncle came to the bus after me, and we then left in the direction of the Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you know about this conversation? Who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My aunt told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many buses did you see at that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were two buses. There were 40 to 45 people on our bus, definitely. It was full of mostly elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you tell whether the second bus was also full?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that it was full, but according to what people said, the bus was roughly as full as the one I was on, so in all there would have been roughly 90 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there only inhabitants of the village present on the bus or were there other people as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people from Erdut were on that bus. There weren't any people from other places.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there were two Arkan's soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were they armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember very well. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did the buses go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out from Erdut on the road to Osijek. Excuse me. We stopped by at Bijelo Brdo. I still don't know why. We were on the bus that stood there for an hour or an hour and a half. And we then proceeded our journey to Osijek past Sarvas without any problems. As we passed Sarvas, we got out of the bus and were told to head on foot towards Nemetin, and it's a small place just outside of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you -- did you stop as you walked towards Nemetin? Did you stop?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right outside of Nemetin, we heard a voice telling us that we should all clear the road and take a canal, a ditch, that was next to the road. We were walking along that ditch for some 50 metres and were then received by soldiers of the Croatian Army or the guard as they were called.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What time of day was this as you're walking?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was getting dark by that point. When we reached Nemetin, it was already dark. We were put up in the cellars of some weekend cottages. We were offered sedatives and drinks and we were waiting for our transportation to Osijek. We were taken there in ambulances. There were several. As soon as we set off for Osijek the shelling of Osijek began and slowed the journey, but it all ended well. We arrived in town specifically at a secondary school for commerce. Our relatives got word of our arrival, and whoever had any relatives there, they would come to pick them up and take them to their homes until they found a place to stay. My brother lived close that school, so I went to his place. My aunt and uncle went to my aunt's brother's -- uncle's house. After a while my aunt and uncle found a place to stay. They moved to that flat, and I joined them later and lived with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you eventually move back to Erdut at some point?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went back -- or, actually, I went to Erdut for the first time again when my aunt died. I think it was in 1999, if I remember correctly, but that was just a short visit to the cemetery, and I returned to my reconstructed house in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you return there to live in 2003?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and I together with our three children. It was the property of my late aunt, and the entire family renounced any rights on that land in favour of me and my brother. And, in fact, since this household lies outside of the village proper it was much harder to rebuilt that property than was the case with the properties in town -- in the village, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time could we please have on the screen 65 -- this would be tab 23, 65 ter 6201.1. And it's described as a list of Dalj residents, and it's dated April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you read the title at the top.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List of persons who were forcibly expelled from the village of Dalj on the 18th of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the Chamber's information, we received this pursuant to an RFA sent to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, do you recognise the markings that appear on this document to the far left?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what are those markings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the initials of my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, for example, the first one, your initials appear at number 3 and it's circled. Why did you put your initials there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man from Dalj. He's one year my junior. I know him from school, from childhood, Antun Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And number 10 also has your initials. Whose name is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Pero Paradzik from Bogaljevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how do you know Pero Paradzik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived across the street from my aunt. He was a neighbour, quite old. He lived a hundred years and died. I knew him from when I was a child.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go through the other names but I also want to make sure that we finish in time, and we only have five minutes. I wanted to ask you, after you reviewed this document did you see your name or the name of your aunt and uncle?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document that is in front of me here, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Is that no to the three names?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So did you see your name on this list?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you see your aunt's name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My aunt's or my uncle's. I didn't see any of the three names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Number 34 is also circled, Hinko Gubina. Who is Hinko Gubina? Is that the same person you mentioned to the Trial Chamber before or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Judging by his first and last name. I did say that I didn't know the person. I don't know where he was from. I recognise the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
